title: Pricing a New SaaS Analytics Product
prompt: Your client is a B2B software company launching a new analytics product for mid-size retailers. They have strong technology but no idea how to price it. How would you help them set a price?
background: The product helps retailers cut inventory waste using demand forecasting.
Target customers are mid-size retailers with $50M-$500M in annual revenue.
The client sells other software to these customers already (existing sales force).
The product is cloud-based; marginal cost to serve one customer is near zero.

clarifying_answers.What is the goal: Maximize profit over three years while gaining a strong foothold.
clarifying_answers.What pricing approaches exist: Cost-plus, competitor-based, and value-based are all on the table.
clarifying_answers.Is there a direct competitor: One competitor charges a flat $40,000/year per customer.

exhibits.name: Customer Value Created
exhibits.description: Estimated annual savings for a typical target customer.
exhibits.data: A typical target customer has $200M revenue and holds inventory equal to 15% of revenue = $30M. The product reduces inventory waste by ~2% of inventory value = $600,000 saved per year per customer.

exhibits.name: Market and Adoption
exhibits.description: Addressable customers and expected adoption at different prices.
exhibits.data: There are 2,000 target retailers. At a $40,000/year price, the client expects 10% adoption (200 customers). Internal research suggests adoption falls to ~5% at $80,000 and rises to ~20% at $20,000.

good_framework: Pricing approaches: cost-plus (irrelevant here, near-zero marginal cost), competitor-based ($40k anchor), value-based (share of value created).
Value to customer: quantify savings created ($600k/year) and capture a defensible share.
Demand / elasticity: adoption at different price points across the 2,000-customer market.
Profit = price x customers adopting; find the revenue-maximizing point given near-zero cost.
Strategy: land-and-expand, bundling with existing software, risk of competitor response.

quant.question: What annual value does the product create for a typical customer?
quant.work: $200M revenue x 15% inventory = $30M inventory; x 2% waste reduction = $600,000/year.

quant.question: Compare annual revenue at $20k, $40k, and $80k given expected adoption.
quant.work: $20k x 20% x 2000 = $8M; $40k x 10% x 2000 = $8M; $80k x 5% x 2000 = $8M. Revenue is similar, so decide on strategy, not just revenue.

quant.question: At the $40k price, what share of the value created is the client capturing?
quant.work: $40,000 price / $600,000 value = ~6.7%, leaving large room to raise price on a value basis.

recommendation: Price on value, not cost or the competitor's anchor. The product creates ~$600k/year of value but the competitor captures only ~7% at $40k. Revenue is similar across price points (~$8M), so use strategy to break the tie: enter near the $40k competitive anchor to win share fast via the existing sales force (land-and-expand), then introduce value-based tiers and premium pricing as ROI is proven. Risk: competitor price war and customers disputing the savings estimate, so build in ROI guarantees or pilots.
